lines.speaker: Daniel
lines.text: Suppose we tried a two-stage method: a three-question paper checklist at the exit and an optional QR follow-up later.

lines.speaker: Aisha
lines.text: What would the second stage add that the paper form doesn’t already collect?

lines.speaker: Daniel
lines.text: If people had another twenty-four hours, they might remember a detail after leaving the building.

lines.speaker: Grace
lines.text: That might work if the QR form asked only two reflection questions. A second full checklist would create duplicate work.

lines.speaker: Aisha
lines.text: What if someone used only the paper form?

lines.speaker: Daniel
lines.text: Their response would still be complete. The QR stage would be optional, not a missing half of the process.

lines.speaker: Grace
lines.text: If we used one anonymous symbol on both forms, we could compare immediate and later comments without collecting names.

lines.speaker: Aisha
lines.text: One possible consequence is that people could think the symbol identifies them.

lines.speaker: Daniel
lines.text: Then we would need a short privacy note explaining that the three symbols are random and contain no personal information.

lines.speaker: Grace
lines.text: Or we could avoid linking the forms at all. We would lose the comparison, but the process would be simpler.

lines.speaker: Aisha
lines.text: I’d prefer the simpler version. If we added tracking before we knew we needed it, we would create an unnecessary privacy concern.

lines.speaker: Daniel
lines.text: Fair point. Suppose the paper form collected the route location, and the optional QR form collected only later reflections.

lines.speaker: Grace
lines.text: In that case, we wouldn’t try to match one person’s two responses. We would compare the kinds of detail each method produces.

lines.speaker: Aisha
lines.text: The downside is extra analysis time. We would have two small sets of comments instead of one.

lines.speaker: Daniel
lines.text: We could test it by making one paper prototype and one two-question QR prototype, then asking three staff members to use both.

lines.speaker: Grace
lines.text: If the same testers used both, we could inspect the response types, but we couldn’t measure natural format preference.

lines.speaker: Aisha
lines.text: Exactly. The test would answer “What detail does each form invite?” not “Which method would visitors choose?”

lines.speaker: Daniel
lines.text: That’s a useful limit. I’ll draft the two prototypes, but I won’t publish or distribute them.

lines.speaker: Grace
lines.text: If the drafts stay anonymous and use only generic route content, I’ll review the questions tomorrow.

lines.speaker: Aisha
lines.text: Good. We’re agreeing to examine a prototype, not to adopt a two-stage public system.
